final_proof:
Let
\[
H=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-,-),\qquad
K=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-,G-),
\]
regarded as functors \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}\). These functors take the object \((D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\) to
\[
H(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD,C),
\qquad
K(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D,GC).
\]
(The local smallness hypotheses ensure that these hom-classes are sets.)

A morphism
\[
u=(f^{\mathrm{op}},g):(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)\longrightarrow
(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)
\]
in the product category consists of \(g:C_1\to C_2\) in \(\mathbf C\) and a morphism \(f^{\mathrm{op}}:D_1^{\mathrm{op}}\to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}\), corresponding to \(f:D_2\to D_1\) in \(\mathbf D\). By the definitions of the hom-bifunctors,
\[
H(u)(h)=g\circ h\circ Ff
\quad\text{for }h:FD_1\to C_1,
\]
whereas
\[
K(u)(k)=Gg\circ k\circ f
\quad\text{for }k:D_1\to GC_1.
\]

Suppose first that Definition 1 holds. Since \(\alpha:H\Rightarrow K\) is a natural isomorphism, its component at each object \(x=(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\),
\[
\alpha_x:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD,C)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D,GC),
\]
is an isomorphism in \(\mathbf{Set}\), and hence a bijection. Naturality at the arbitrary morphism \(u=(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\) above says
\[
\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}\circ H(u)
=
K(u)\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}.
\]
Using the displayed formulas for \(H(u)\) and \(K(u)\), this is exactly
\[
\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}
 \circ\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^{\mathrm{op}},g)
=
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^{\mathrm{op}},Gg)
 \circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)},
\]
with the two horizontal maps acting respectively by
\[
h\longmapsto g\circ h\circ Ff,
\qquad
k\longmapsto Gg\circ k\circ f.
\]
This is precisely the commutative-square condition in Definition 2. Thus Definition 1 implies Definition 2.

Conversely, suppose Definition 2 holds. For every object \(x=(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\), let \(\alpha_x:H(x)\to K(x)\) be the specified bijection. Every morphism of \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C\) is a pair \(u=(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\), and the equality in Definition 2 is precisely
\[
\alpha_y\circ H(u)=K(u)\circ\alpha_x
\qquad\text{for every }u:x\to y.
\]
Therefore the family \((\alpha_x)_x\) is a natural transformation \(\alpha:H\Rightarrow K\).

Finally, this natural transformation is a natural isomorphism. Indeed, each \(\alpha_x\) is bijective, so define \(\beta_x=\alpha_x^{-1}:K(x)\to H(x)\). For any \(u:x\to y\), naturality of \(\alpha\) gives
\[
\alpha_yH(u)=K(u)\alpha_x.
\]
Composing on the left by \(\alpha_y^{-1}\) and on the right by \(\alpha_x^{-1}\) gives
\[
H(u)\beta_x=\beta_yK(u),
\]
which is exactly the naturality condition for \(\beta:K\Rightarrow H\). Moreover,
\[
\beta_x\alpha_x=\operatorname{id}_{H(x)}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\alpha_x\beta_x=\operatorname{id}_{K(x)}
\]
for every \(x\). Hence \(\beta\) is a two-sided inverse to \(\alpha\), so \(\alpha\) is a natural isomorphism. This is Definition 1, and therefore the two definitions are equivalent.
